outputs.L1:
Because the original text is deeply poetic, surreal, and evocative—reminiscent of modern confessional poetry—a standard corporate polish would strip away its artistic power. 

Below are two polished versions that elevate the grammar, flow, and literary elegance while preserving **every piece of imagery, emotion, and detail** from your original text.

---

### Option 1: Elevated Literary Prose (Smooth & Fluid)
> First, the fatherly trellis of my voice—or perhaps my noose—abruptly vanished. Now, I wear this razor-sharp fishhook of a crucifix. Look at how it forces my head downward in shame—and yet, in glory. Behold this frail, weightless chain; there is another just like it. At times, my neck feels as though it is breaking under its weight. 
> 
> It rests here, adjacent to the heart’s hidden chamber, where a table is prepared for me instead of a dark bar. No longer must I endure that meaningless horror. It is a chain both weightless and frail, yet heavy as a massive iron anchor draped in seaweed and bearded with barnacles. 
> 
> Toward dawn, you might peer through your door and see me struggling to reach the end of the hallway, bent double and taking small, desperate sips of air. Yet I will make it there, to a table set for three: the Unseen Host, myself, and my own glorified body. He vaguely resembles me, though he is neither radiant nor splendid. He is ugly, bearing the countenance of someone who has wept his entire life. *"That cannot be my soul,"* people scream when they first behold it.

---

### Option 2: Polished Prose Poem (Rhythmic & Stylized)
> First, the trellis of my voice—or noose—abruptly vanished. Now I wear this razory fishhook of a crucifix. 
> 
> Look how it helps me keep my head bowed down in shame, yet crowned in glory. See this frail, weightless chain: there is another just like it. At times, my neck feels as though it is breaking. It hangs right here, near the heart’s hidden room, where a table is set for me rather than a dark bar. No more of that pointless horror. A weightless, frail chain—yet a massive iron anchor, seaweed-draped and barnacle-bearded. 
> 
> Toward dawn, you may peek from your doorway and watch me attempting to reach the end of the hallway, bent double and gasping for air in small sips. But I will arrive. There will be a table set for three: the Unseen Host, myself, and my glorified body. He resembles me only vaguely, offering no radiance or splendor; he is ugly, as though he has spent a lifetime weeping. 
> 
> *"That cannot be my soul!"* people cry when they first catch sight of him.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Punctuation & Flow:** Resolved run-on sentences and fragmented numbers, replacing them with intentional pauses (dashes, semicolons, and periods) to enhance the dramatic cadence.
* **Grammar & Clarity:** Smoothed phrasing like *"razory fishhook of crucifix"* to *"razor-sharp fishhook of a crucifix"* and clarified transitions without altering the unique, striking metaphors.
* **Formatting:** Grouped the thoughts into coherent thematic beats (the spiritual weight, the physical struggle, and the surreal encounter at the table).
outputs.L2:
Here is a complete rewrite of the text, maintaining every original detail and idea through entirely new phrasing and sentence structures:

***

Without warning, the paternal framework that once sustained—or perhaps suffocated—my words vanished entirely. In its place, I now wear a sharp, fishhook-like crucifix around my neck. Observe how this emblem forces me to bow my head low, weighed down by a blend of divine majesty and deep remorse. Take note of this delicate, featherlight necklace; it has an invisible counterpart. At times, the burden is so intense that my cervical spine feels as though it is about to snap. 

The cross rests directly over the concealed chamber of my chest, where a place is set for a meal rather than a seat at a dimly lit tavern. That meaningless nightmare has finally ended. Though the physical necklace seems thin and fragile, its spiritual counterpart acts like an enormous iron anchor, heavy with marine growth and covered in barnacles. 

If you were to peer into the hallway around daybreak, you might catch a glimpse of me struggling toward the bathroom, folded completely in half and desperately swallowing tiny gasps of air. Nevertheless, I will arrive at the spot where a table is prepared for a trio: the invisible Lord, my present self, and my resurrected form. This transcendent version of me bears only a vague resemblance to my physical face and possesses no dazzling splendour or beauty. Instead, he appears hideous, marked by what looks like an eternity of endless weeping—a sight so grotesque that onlookers shriek in disbelief that such an unsightly figure could possibly be my spirit.
outputs.L3:
I walk beneath the crush of an invisible, agony-laden weight—a spiritual burden so profound it bends my spine and forces my eyes downward in shame. It is a heavy, suffocating presence, compelling me to bow my head as if to hide from the gaze of heaven, unable to lift my face against the shadow of my own transgressions.

Yet, despite this crush, I am trying to turn away. I am striving to sever myself from the twilight world I once inhabited—a shadowland of dimly lit bars, wasted nights, and the senseless horror of a life squandered in dark corners. Before me now lies a new path, clean and meticulously prepared, offering the quiet promise of order and redemption. I fix my focus on this narrow corridor, desperate to leave the chaotic filth of my past behind.

To walk this new road, however, is a brutal endeavor. My flesh rebels against the journey; severe physical agony and utter exhaustion claim every inch of my body. My lungs seize, leaving me gasping for air as if the very act of breathing were a privilege I no longer deserve. Even the simplest movements—shifting a limb, taking a single step forward—require an agonizing act of sheer will, forcing me to confront the profound fragility of my physical frame.

When I finally reach the end of my strength and confront my own soul, expecting to find the promised light of spiritual renewal, the illusion shatters. I had hoped to behold a "glorified body"—a radiant, transcendent form purified of mortal decay. Instead, I stand face-to-face with a heartbreaking reality: my soul is deeply, permanently scarred. It stands before me not in shining glory, but broken and weeping, bearing the raw, unhealed wounds of a lifetime of pain.
outputs.L4:
For years, the poison was not merely in my veins; it was the architecture of my chest, a heavy, calcified cage built from years of deceit, compulsions, and blackouts. Addiction is a coward’s bargain—it promises oblivion but collects its tax in ghost-weight guilt that settles deeper with every stolen high. When the breaking point finally arrived, it came not as a soft realization, but as an intolerable weight. I knew that if I was to survive, I had to burn away the rot. I needed a pilgrimage of raw, unmitigated penance.

I fled to the high, barren stone of the wilderness, leaving behind every comfort that had ever served as a warm blanket over my decay. The ordeal began in the dark. 

Withdrawal was a physical crucifixion. My muscles tore against themselves; my skin felt scorched by cold air, itching with phantom cravings that shrieked for release. In the fever-dream nights, sweating through wool blankets on the frozen ground, the guilt took physical shape. Every promise I had broken, every person I had hollowed out to feed my sickness stood over me in the shadows. I welcomed the agony. I dragged my trembling body up mountain trails, starving out the addiction, letting the bitter wind scourge my face until I bled. 

I endured the physical nightmare because I was driven by a single, desperate fantasy: I believed that on the other side of this torment lay my glorified soul. I envisioned it as an ethereal sanctuary—a radiant, untainted version of myself. I pictured a being made of light and marble, polished clean by my suffering, standing immaculate and victorious over the ash of my past. I believed I was earning a holy perfection.

On the seventh night, at the peak of the fever and the apex of my fast, the veil tore open. In the center of a silent, moonlit clearing, I met the entity I had suffered to see.

I stepped forward, ready to kneel before my golden, redeemed self. But as the silhouette took shape, my breath hitched, and horror seized my throat.

There was no light. There was no marble. 

Sitting in the dust was a figure grotesque and harrowing to behold. Its skin was bruised and mottled, raw like an open wound exposed to the salt of the earth. Its limbs were bent, its frame stooped beneath invisible beams, and its face was a landscape of deep, agonizing lines. It was not shining; it was shuddering. And from its sunken, dark eyes wept an endless stream of silent, burning tears.

"Is this my reward?" I cried out to the empty night, my voice cracking with betrayal. "I stripped my flesh to the bone for *this*? I broke myself to meet a monster?"

I collapsed before the shivering thing, weeping in rage and disappointment. But as I lay in the dirt, the creature reached out. Its hands were rough, scarred, and trembling, but its touch upon my forehead was impossibly tender. 

It was then, in the suffocating quiet, that the truth flooded into me like cold river water.

This was not a monster. This was my soul—unburdened by the anesthesia of addiction for the first time in a decade. The gold and marble I had lusted after was just another lie, another high, another slick illusion to hide from reality. Perfection was an ideal for angels who had never bled; it had nothing to do with a man who had crawled out of the gutter.

This weeping, bruised thing was beautiful because it was *real*. It was ugly because it bore the honest weight of everything I had done, everything I had survived, and everything I had felt and buried. The tears it shed were not tears of defeat, but the first clean water to run through my spirit in a lifetime. The numbness was gone. The heart was beating again, even if it beat in pain.

I realized then that spiritual redemption is not a magic act that transmutes dirt into gold. It does not erase the scars; it teaches them how to speak. True grace is not found in an ideal perfection, but in the willingness to sit in the dust, embrace your raw, unvarnished suffering, and hold the hand of the weeping, broken thing you truly are—sober, present, and finally alive.
outputs.L5:
When I was young, I used to sit on an upside-down paint bucket in the corner of the garage and just watch. My **father** had a way of moving through his work with a quiet, deliberate patience that felt almost holy. He didn't speak much while he worked, but every movement was a silent lesson waiting to be gathered.

"**Look** closely," he would say softly, gesturing toward the intricate grain of a piece of oak or the subtle alignment of a machine's gears. "If you don't take the time to understand **how** something is built, you’ll never know how to mend it when it breaks." 

Back then, I thought he was only teaching me about carpentry and engines. I didn't realize he was actually offering a blueprint for life—teaching me that difficult problems require patience, and that the most meaningful things are built with intention.

Decades later, I found myself standing in my own workshop, struggling with a project that refused to go right. Frustration flared, and I was ready to throw my hands up. But as I leaned against the workbench, I caught my reflection in the dusty windowpane. The set of my shoulders, the slight tilt of my head, the way my hands rested on the wood—it was like seeing a ghost. 

In that moment, I remembered his voice. I took a deep breath, picked up my tools, and began again. It is remarkable **how** love translates across time—not always through grand speeches, but through the quiet habits passed down from a **father** to a child who simply knew enough to **look**, listen, and learn.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal poem about early addiction recovery, guilt, and religious imagery in the style of Franz Wright.
counterfactuals.output:
**Liturgy of the Tremor**

Day four.
The sun enters the room like a doctor 
who has already given up on the patient.

I am sitting on the edge of the mattress,
my hands fluttering—
two wild, filthy birds 
trapped inside a cathedral of bone.

Lord of the cold tap,
Lord of the linoleum floor.
Forgive me. 
The poison was the only thing 
that spoke to me in your voice.

In the corner, an angel made of wet ash
is eating my old addresses.
It does not look at me.
It knows what I did to the light.

When I close my eyes,
the spoon is still glowing in the dark,
a little moon I held in my lap
to keep from dying of the cold.
Now the cold is back,
and it has brought its friends:
every person I ever lied to,
standing silently at the foot of the bed,
their faces turned into blank mirrors.

I try to remember the Lord’s Prayer,
but all that comes up is sweat.
A sour, yellow baptism.
My skin is too thin now—
I can hear the worms talking in the yard,
I can hear the light screaming as it touches the windowpane.

Is this what it means to be saved?
To be flayed alive in a quiet room,
holding a glass of water that weighs
as much as a church?

If you are there,
do not come any closer.
I am still covered in the dark.
Just leave a little silence on the table—
not grace, not yet,
just the permission 
to breathe without bleeding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short prose poem divided into numbered sections that explores the physical agony of sobriety. Incorporate images of a heavy crucifix, an anchor, a quiet hallway at dawn, and an ugly, weeping soul instead of a radiant one.
counterfactuals.output:
**1.**
Dawn bleeds into the quiet hallway, pale and merciless. The silence does not soothe; it hums with the high, terrible pitch of raw nerve endings waking from their dull sleep. The floor beneath bare feet is an anvil. Sobriety begins not with clarity, but with the body revolting against its own pulse—a cold sweat that smells of copper, a stomach hollowed by phantom spasms, and a jaw clamped so tight the teeth ache down to the root.

**2.**
They speak of lightness, but the chest collapses under the mass of a sunken anchor. It sits heavy in the gut, dragged through the dark silt of the throat with every dry, rattling breath. Pressed flat against the sternum rests a crucifix of unpolished iron—not a symbol of grace, but a dead weight bruising the ribs, holding the body pinned to the cold linoleum. To be clean is to be anchored to the earth by pain alone, nailed to the hard surface of the present hour.

**3.**
Peeled back from the warm, liquid fog, the soul is not a radiant bird or a gentle flame. It is an ugly, weeping thing, shivering in the dark cavity beneath the breastbone. It is slick, raw-skinned, and malformed, clutching its bruised knees as it cringes from the light. It has no beauty, no holy sheen; it is only a pathetic, writhing knot of nerves, crying out in terror because it can finally feel everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you give me a raw, stream-of-consciousness piece about a man walking down a hallway at night while suffering from withdrawal? He should be reflecting on leaving dark bars behind, carrying a metaphorical heavy chain, and meeting his own pitiful, un-glorified body.
counterfactuals.output:
Left, right, left, no, wait, the floor is tilting, carpet’s wet under the socks or maybe that’s just the sweat dripping off my heels, god it’s cold, why am I sweating if the air is like knives? Buzzing. The light overhead is buzzing, a sickly butter-yellow tube flickering *bzzzt-bzzzt* like a dying wasp in a glass jar. Hold the wall. Drywall rough under the knuckles, dragging a red line behind me, maybe, don't look back. 

Bone-deep. It’s in the marrow. Ice water in the veins and kerosene in the gut and every single hair on my arms standing up screaming for a drop, just a splash, half an inch in a sticky glass. 

No. No more. 

Left the dark behind. Left the neon bleeding into the rain outside the dive, the red *OPEN* sign flickering like a pulse I couldn't keep up with. God, the dark bars. I miss them. I hate them. That warm, thick, stale-beer darkness where nobody looks at your face, where the pine-sol and bad whiskey cover up the smell of dying inside. You could just sink into the vinyl booth, sink into the wood, let the amber wash the sharp edges off the world until everything was round and soft and didn't hurt. But the dark started biting back. It wasn't a cloak anymore, it was a mouth. I walked out. Stepped out of the cave into the night and now I’m here, trapped in this endless, sterile, three-a.m. hallway, and the dark isn't back there, it's inside my ribs.

Heavy. Jesus, why is it so heavy to take a step?

Dragging it. Every step a clank, a scrape, iron on carpet. I can feel it wrapped around my sternum, looping down the spine, heavy links forged glass by glass, shot by shot, year by year. A chain. A real, black-iron bastard of a chain dragging ten feet behind me, pulling me back toward the stairs, back toward the street, back toward the corner where the neon bleeds. *Clack-scrape.* It’s pulling my shoulders down, caving my chest in. Can't breathe. Air is too thin. Too dry. Tastes like cardboard and old copper.

The nausea rolls up—hot salt at the back of the tongue. Hold it. Swallow it. Don't throw up on the runner. 

There's the hall mirror. By the bathroom door. 

Don't look. 

I look.

Christ. 

Where’s the tragic hero? Where’s the brooding poet starving in the attic? Nowhere. Just this. Just a pitiful, un-glorified sack of wet sticks and grey meat. Look at it. Trembling. A rat in a bucket. White scum dried at the corners of the mouth, skin the color of lard, sunken dark bruises under eyes that can’t focus, pupils pinned or blown, who knows, who cares. Sweat soaking through the grey t-shirt, sticking it to ribs that look like a starved dog's. Trembling so hard the teeth are clicking—*clack-clack-clack*—a pathetic little percussion section in a mouth that tastes like rot. No glory in this. No poetry in shivering so hard your thighs cramp. Just a body. A broken, demanding, ugly machine running out of juice, turning on itself, chewing its own wires.

It’s just meat that hurts. 

Look at yourself, you bastard. Look at what’s left when the booze drains out. 

The reflection shakes, blurs. Another wave of ice washes down my neck. The chain tugs, heavy iron link slamming against the ankle bone. Step. Keep walking. Pass the mirror. Leave the ghost behind. Just the hall, the yellow light, the carpet, the sweat, the long cold walk to a bed I won't sleep in. Left. Right. Drag the iron. Step.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surreal prose poem containing the following motifs: a broken voice, a weightless chain that feels like an anchor, a table set for three, and a soul that frightens people because it looks like it has been crying all its life.
counterfactuals.output:
The soul walks through the pale market with its skin draped like damp linen, and the villagers bolt their shutters against it. They are not afraid of violence, but of its terrible, waterlogged glow—they turn away because the soul looks as though it has been weeping since the day the first sun was struck from the dark, its edges perpetually dissolved by a tide of ancient salt. 

Around its throat drifts a chain woven of dry air and helium. It possesses no weight at all; it floats upward toward the rafters like thin smoke, yet it drags upon the soul with the suffocating pressure of a iron anchor dropped into the bottomless trench of a sky. 

In the center of a room where the wallpaper bleeds red clover, a table is set for three. Three fine porcelain plates sit empty, catching the dust of falling moths: one plate for the memory, one for the shadow, and one for the body that refused to arrive. The soul pulls itself into the central chair, the weightless links tugging its head down toward the wood as if tethering a drowning swimmer to the floorboards.

It tries to call out across the cloth, to welcome the missing, but its broken voice splinters against the empty air. What leaves its throat is not sound, but a brittle cascade of rusted needles and dry cicada wings that shatter before reaching the third napkin. The salt on the soul’s face slowly fills the water glasses, one drop at a time, until the room begins to float away on a sea of old grief.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a monologue from the perspective of someone trying to make it to the bathroom during a painful morning after quitting alcohol. Use surreal and visceral imagery to contrast the traditional ideas of religious salvation with the grim reality of human suffering and self-loathing.
counterfactuals.output:
They preach about the washing of the feet. They talk about baptism, about dipping into clear, running waters and rising up clean, white as wool, newborn under a benevolent sun. 

They lie. 

Salvation isn't a river. It’s ten feet of brown, stained carpet between this bed and the hallway door, and right now, every fiber of that carpet is a standing needle, and my body is a sack of wet glass breaking from the inside out. 

Don't open your eyes. Don't—*god*, the light through the blinds isn't light at all; it’s liquid nickel, pouring straight into my retinas, boiling the brain inside the skull. 

I roll off the mattress. I hit the floor with a sound like a dropped side of beef. Is this the mortification of the flesh? Is this the holy fire? My sheets are twisted around my knees, a damp, sour shroud. Lazarus didn't smell like this when he stepped out of the tomb. He didn't smell like sweat that turned into vinegar overnight, like stale grain and copper and dead cells bleeding through the pores. 

My heart is a trapped bird, beating three hundred times a minute against my ribs, smashing its wings against the bone. *Thump-thump-thump.* A hammer in an empty chapel. 

I begin to crawl. 

elbow over elbow. The carpet scrapes the skin off my forearms, but I can’t feel the pain properly—it’s muffled, smothered under the static buzzing in my blood. My liver feels like an iron ember, tucked right under my ribs, glowing red, cooking me from the center. *Transubstantiation.* Isn't that what they call it? The miracle where the bread turns to flesh, the wine turns to blood? I did that. I did it every night for five years. I drank the blood of the grape until my own blood turned to acid, and now my veins are screaming for the poison that quieted them.

*Five feet left.* 

My throat twitches. A dry heave catches me in the gut, bending me double on the floorboards, a violent, involuntary bow to a god of trash and dust. Nothing comes up yet—just a wave of bitter heat, the taste of rust and bile on the back of my tongue. 

They promised a still, small voice. Where is it? All I hear is a frequency, a high-pitched, electric shriek ringing in my ears, the sound of my nervous system snapping its own wires. They tell you that hitting rock bottom is a spiritual awakening. They print it on pamphlets with pictures of mountains and sunbursts. They don't tell you about the tremors. They don't tell you that your hands will shake so hard you can’t grip the doorframe, that your fingers look like pale, dying spiders twitching on the baseboard.

I reach the doorway. I drag my torso over the cold, hard brass of the threshold. 

The bathroom. 

The white linoleum is ice against my cheek. I lay there for a second, pressed against the floor, listening to the hum of the pipes inside the wall. It sounds like an organ playing a hymn for nobody. 

I pull myself up by the lip of the basin. My reflection catches me in the mirror, but that’s not a soul made in the divine image. That’s a hollowed-out turnip. Gray skin, purple hollows beneath eyes that look like boiled eggs. A mouth caked with white salt.

I drop to my knees before the porcelain bowl. 

The classic posture. The holy position. Kneeling before the altar. 

I grip the cold rim. My knuckles turn white. The porcelain is the only clean thing left in the universe, immaculate, frigid, waiting to receive my confession. 

And then the grace hits me. 

Not a dove descending from the clouds. Not a warm light wrapping around my shoulders. Just a violent, agonizing spasm that tears through my diaphragm, forcing my jaws apart. I purge. It comes out of me in hot, yellow streams—pure gall, wormwood, the bitter, putrid sludge of a body trying to eject its own rot. I heave until my abdominal muscles feel like shredded ropes, until my eyes bleed tears, until I’m coughing up thin strings of blood into the water.

When it stops, I don't feel reborn. I don't feel redeemed. 

I just feel empty. A scraped-out shell resting its forehead against the freezing porcelain, shivering in my own cold sweat, smelling the stench of my own survival. 

No angels came. No choir sang. 

Just me, choking on the floor, waiting for the shaking to stop.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
